paragraphs.source_en: In the Tassili, paintings are usually accumulated in selected areas but not outside them, i. e. the paintings are not disseminated across a vast territory but they are concentrated in some areas and the territory between painted sites is generally devoid of images even if there are suitable shelters. The norm is that in a suitable site there are either a great number of paintings or nothing at all. It is therefore evident that sites containing paintings attracted other images which were added to already existing figures, either next to them or superimposed on them. Different Round Head styles found often on a wall or in a site suggest a frequentation of the place during a certain period. So why was a site repeatedly visited? The creation of a new painting was unlikely to have been made without purpose.

paragraphs.source_en: Supposing that the image and/or the act of painting had a deeper meaning, this would mean that the painted sites were probably cultic places. In this sense empty sites may be explained-they were not cultic places. Thus, a site itself was important for the fact that it was, especially in the Tassili, selected among other suitable sites.

paragraphs.source_en: The paintings themselves suggest that painted sites were not used for everyday life activities. The occurrence of body paintings and horned figures is high and they occur in the majority of sites. Prehistoric huntergatherers were unlikely to wear horns (or other appendages on the head) or masks in their ordinary life, but they probably adorned themselves for special occasions. These occasions could have been rituals, rites or ceremonies similar to those documented in the ethnographic record of modern African hunter-gatherer societies (e. g. Silberbauer 1965; Lee 1979). Round Head paintings often represent what can be described as dances and also individuals in a particular posture definable as worshipping.
